system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2131-04-17 14:41:00 to 2131-04-19 14:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, bipolar disorder, PTSD, and multiple abdominal surgeries was admitted for acute exacerbation of chronic abdominal pain following consumption of a deviled egg. He presented with severe mid-abdominal pain radiating to the left, consistent with prior pancreatitis flares. Initial concern for internal hernia was ruled out by surgery based on CT findings. The patient was managed conservatively with NPO status for two days, IV fluids, IV pain control with Dilaudid, and anti-nausea medication. He gradually advanced to a regular low-fat diet and transitioned to oral pain medications. His pain improved to baseline, and he remained stable without complications. He was discharged home with updated pain and enzyme medications, instructions for low-fat diet, and follow-up with primary care.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis

abdominal surgeries who now presents with abdominal pain.

COMPARISONS:  Chest radiographs of ___.

FINDINGS:

Frontal and lateral views of the chest demonstrate normal lung volumes without
pleural effusion, focal consolidation or pneumothorax.  Hilar and mediastinal
silhouettes are unremarkable.  The heart size is normal.  There is no
pulmonary edema.  There is no free air under diaphragms.

IMPRESSION:

No evidence of acute cardiopulmonary process.

INDICATION:  Patient with chronic pancreatitis and multiple prior surgeries,
now presents with abdominal pain.  Assess for obstruction.

COMPARISONS:  CT abdomen of ___ and abdominal radiographs of
___.

FINDINGS:

Supine and upright views of the abdomen demonstrate several air-fluid levels
and a prominent loop of small bowel in the left upper quadrant.  Increased
fecal matter is seen in the proximal colon compared to what is usually
expected.  There is a general paucity of small bowel gas as well as gas in the
distal colon.  There is no pneumatosis or free air.  Multiple surgical clips
and sutures chains project over right mid and upper abdomen.  No soft tissue
mass or soft calcifications seen.  Visualized lung bases are clear.  Osseous
structures appear intact.

IMPRESSION:

Several air-fluid levels and a prominent loop of small bowel in the left upper
quadrant, probably the site of an ___ represent early small-bowel
obstruction but findngs are highly non-specific particularly with a general
paucity of small bowel gas and an ileus could also be considered.  Increased
amount of fecal matter in the proximal colon.

INDICATION:  ___ male with chronic pancreatitis.  For interval
evaluation.

EXAMINATION:  Supine and erect abdominal radiographs.

COMPARISONS:  ___ and ___.

FINDINGS:  There are several scattered nonspecific prominent loops of
gas-containing small bowel within the left upper and mid abdomen without
evidence of frank dilation to indicate obstruction.  These appear slightly
more conspicuous since prior examination.  Clips overlie the right upper
quadrant.  There is no evidence of pneumatosis, portal venous air, or
pneumoperitoneum.  There is left basilar atelectasis with the lung bases
otherwise being clear.  Sequela of prior abdominal hernia repair is
demonstrated projecting in the mid abdomen.  The visualized osseous structures
are intact.

IMPRESSION:  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern without definite evidence of
obstruction.

INDICATION:  History of chronic pancreatitis and multiple abdominal surgeries
with acute on chronic abdominal pain.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector helical CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was
obtained after the administration of 130 cc IV Omnipaque contrast and oral
contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformations were prepared.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior examinations, most recent CT dated ___ and correlation with radiograph of the same date.

FINDINGS:  The included portions of the lung bases are clear with mild
dependent atelectatic changes.  There are coronary artery calcifications.

Within the abdomen, multiple fluid-filled loops of small bowel are seen;
however, no evidence of obstruction is present.  There are multiple prominent
mesenteric lymph nodes, likely reactive.  The post-surgical appearance of the
bowel is not significantly changed from the prior examination.

The pancreas is atrophic with multiple punctate calcifications consistent with
history of chronic pancreatitis.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy. 
The bladder, spleen, adrenal glands, and left kidney are grossly unremarkable.
The right kidney contains multiple hypodensities, too small to characterize,
however, unchanged from the prior exam.

Within the pelvis, distal loops of large bowel and rectum are normal in size
and caliber.  The bladder, distal ureters and prostate gland appear grossly
unremarkable.  No free air or free fluid is seen.

No concerning osseous lesion is seen.

The patient is status post Puestow procedure.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence of obstruction.  Nonspecific fluid within the small bowel. 
Multiple prominent mesenteric lymph nodes, likely reactive.

2.  Findings consistent with history of chronic pancreatitis including atrophy
and pancreatic calcifications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. Can you tell me about the pain you're having?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s back, same as before—sharp pain in my upper belly, going to the left side. Feels just like my last flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just at the start, but not now. I’ve been passing gas and having loose stools, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps rule out a blockage. You mentioned you’ve had blood in your urine recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a few days ago, but it went away on its own. No burning or urgency now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We’ll check a urine test just in case, but since it resolved, it may not be urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is this another pancreatitis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks that way. Your CT scan shows changes consistent with chronic pancreatitis—calcifications and atrophy of the pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of obstruction. There are some air-fluid levels, but they’re nonspecific—could be from slowed bowel movement due to pain or meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much because of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll keep you NPO for now—no food by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? How long will that be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually 24 to 48 hours. We’ll give you IV fluids and pain meds. Once the pain settles, we’ll start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been using Dilaudid at home. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV Dilaudid now for better control. Once you’re eating, we’ll switch back to oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds? I take metformin and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been low—between 60 and 90—because you’re not eating. We’ve held both the insulin and metformin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart them when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only when you’re eating regularly again and your sugars are above 130. We’ll write that in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as intense. Can I try some food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids—broth, apple juice—and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any chance this was something else, like a bowel blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were concerned at first, but the CT showed no obstruction. The bowel gas pattern is nonspecific, likely due to the flare-up and reduced intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart and lungs? The chest X-ray okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chest X-ray was clear—no pneumonia, fluid, or free air. All stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been feeling anxious with the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed you were tearful yesterday. As your pain improves, your mood seems better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s hard when the pain’s bad. I take duloxetine and lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your lorazepam, and we’re adjusting your duloxetine dose down to 30 mg daily for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to minimize side effects while you’re recovering. You can discuss adjusting it back with your psychiatrist if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Pain is much improved, and you’ve tolerated a regular diet since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re discharging you with a few days of oral Dilaudid for pain, and Miralax to prevent constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pancreas enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue taking three capsules with meals. Also keep up the omeprazole and low-fat diet to reduce strain on your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your primary care provider to monitor your blood sugars and restart your diabetes meds when appropriate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I’ll avoid alcohol and driving while on the Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call us if the pain worsens or you develop fever, vomiting, or dark urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Get some rest and follow the instructions closely.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and multiple abdominal surgeries was admitted for acute on chronic abdominal pain. The pain was consistent with a flare of chronic pancreatitis, without evidence of obstruction on CT imaging. He was managed supportively with NPO status, IV fluids, and IV pain control, then advanced to a regular diet as symptoms improved. His blood sugars were low due to poor oral intake, prompting temporary discontinuation of insulin and metformin. Pain and mood improved during the stay. He was discharged home with oral pain medication, Miralax, continued pancreatic enzymes, and instructions to restart diabetes medications when eating normally and blood sugars exceed 130, along with follow-up in outpatient care.
